body.statement: For every \(\vartheta\in\mathcal F_B(p)\) in the no-selection overlap satisfying \(\mathcal K_{\mathrm K}(P_{\vartheta})\), the simultaneous equations in the proof of Kawakami (2021), Theorem 1 on pages 12135--12137 identify \(\omega_0^{\mathrm K}\) and \(\omega_1^{\mathrm K}\). If \(\mathcal T_B(p)\) is a singleton, its atlas value agrees with \(\tau(\vartheta)=\phi_{\mathrm K}(\omega_0^{\mathrm K},\omega_1^{\mathrm K})\). Kawakami's identified scope is the four joint probabilities of binary potential-outcome types, together with their treatment-conditional weights used for PN and PS, under Figure 2(b), equation (2), and Theorem 1(i)--(iii). For the single explicit selected boundary datum \((p^{\mathrm{bd}},m^{\mathrm{bd}})\), \(\mathcal F_A(p^{\mathrm{bd}},m^{\mathrm{bd}})\ne\varnothing\) and \(\mathcal T_A(p^{\mathrm{bd}},m^{\mathrm{bd}})=\{(1/2,1/2)\}\), but \(A_x^{\mathrm K}(b^{\mathrm{bd}})\) is singular for each \(x\): because \(\mathcal W=\{w_1,w_2,w_3\}\), its first column is the sum of its last three columns. Thus this legal selected response-cycle law violates the named invertibility assumption in Kawakami's Theorem 1(i) while remaining classified by the atlas; this is a strict scope separation, not a subsumption claim.
body.justification: This supporting theorem records the exact no-selection IV-plus-proxy overlap and a one-law separation from Kawakami's regular invertibility domain.
body.gap: Kawakami (2021), Figure 2(b), equation (2), Theorem 1(i)--(iii), and its appendix identify all four response-type probabilities under invertible proxy-loading and observable blocks plus cross-treatment separation, but do not classify selected or singular response-cycle fibers.
body.consumer: IV-plus-proxy analysts can audit agreement on Kawakami-regular laws and recognize a concrete selected boundary law for which the regular matrix method is unavailable but the atlas still returns an exact certificate.
body.proof_tex:
Fix \(\vartheta\in\mathcal F_B(p)\) in the stated no-selection overlap and
suppose \(\mathcal K_{\mathrm K}(P_{\vartheta})\).  The cited Kawakami
identification lemma applies because the factorization, invertibilities,
cross-treatment separation, and structural exclusion conditions are exactly
those recorded by \(\mathcal K_{\mathrm K}\).  It identifies the two
treatment-conditional response-type vectors \(\omega_0^{\mathrm K}\) and
\(\omega_1^{\mathrm K}\) by the simultaneous equations in the proof of its
Theorem 1.

In the order \((00,01,10,11)\), response consistency implies that
\((X,Y)=(1,1)\) admits exactly types \(01\) and \(11\), while
\((X,Y)=(0,0)\) admits exactly types \(00\) and \(01\).  The positive
selected cells and \(S=1\) almost surely make both conditioning events have
positive probability.  Therefore Bayes' rule gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathrm{PN}(\vartheta)
 &=\frac{\omega^{\mathrm K}_{1,2}}
         {\omega^{\mathrm K}_{1,2}+\omega^{\mathrm K}_{1,4}},\\
 \mathrm{PS}(\vartheta)
 &=\frac{\omega^{\mathrm K}_{0,2}}
         {\omega^{\mathrm K}_{0,1}+\omega^{\mathrm K}_{0,2}}.
 \end{aligned} \tag{34}
\]
By the definition of \(\phi_{\mathrm K}\), equation (34) is
\[
 \tau(\vartheta)
 =\phi_{\mathrm K}(\omega_0^{\mathrm K},\omega_1^{\mathrm K}). \tag{35}
\]
If \(\mathcal T_B(p)\) is a singleton, it contains \(\tau(\vartheta)\) by
definition.  The full-rigidity theorem makes the atlas return that unique
element, and hence (35).  The cited result identifies all four binary
potential-outcome-type probabilities and the conditional weights appearing
in (34); this establishes the stated description of its scope.

For the separate scope witness, every row of
\(A_x^{\mathrm K}(b^{\mathrm{bd}})\) has the form
\[
 \bigl(1,b_i^{\mathrm{bd}}(w_1),
          b_i^{\mathrm{bd}}(w_2),b_i^{\mathrm{bd}}(w_3)\bigr). \tag{36}
\]
Since \(b_i^{\mathrm{bd}}\) is a probability vector on three points, the
last three entries of (36) sum to one.  Thus, for each \(x\), the first
column of \(A_x^{\mathrm K}(b^{\mathrm{bd}})\) is the sum of its last three
columns, and
\[
 \det A_x^{\mathrm K}(b^{\mathrm{bd}})=0. \tag{37}
\]
The experimental-overlap and boundary-separation theorem has already proved
\[
 \mathcal F_A(p^{\mathrm{bd}},m^{\mathrm{bd}})\ne\varnothing,
 \qquad
 \mathcal T_A(p^{\mathrm{bd}},m^{\mathrm{bd}})
 =\{(1/2,1/2)\}. \tag{38}
\]
Consequently this legal selected response-cycle law is exactly classified by
the atlas, but (37) violates the named invertibility premise in Kawakami's
Theorem 1(i).  This single-law witness proves strict scope separation; it does
not assert that either result subsumes the other.
